title: Thomson Reuters Survey: Over 95% of Legal Professionals Expect Gen AI to Become Central to Workflow Within Five Years
author: Robert Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports AI as augmentation and documents policy and training gaps, but it addresses law-firm adoption rather than direct-to-consumer legal assistance, users’ verification capacity, access-to-justice outcomes or the downward transfer of risk. It therefore does not establish a clear position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core framing of AI as augmenting legal expertise and reshaping established workflows rather than replacing lawyers wholesale. It materially extends the synthesis with adoption evidence showing that organisational policy, training and ROI measurement lag behind use, reinforcing the importance of organisational complements, although it provides little direct evidence on verification or apprenticeship risks.

kp.k: Survey covers multiple professions, with legal respondents a minority
kp.d: Ambrogi reports findings from the Thomson Reuters Institute's 2025 Generative AI in Professional Services Report. Its survey included 1,702 respondents across seven sectors, with data collected in January and February 2025; legal professionals represented 41% of respondents. These sample boundaries distinguish profession-wide findings from legal-specific results.
qs: The Thomson Reuters Institute survey included 1,702 respondents across legal, tax, accounting, audit, corporate risk, fraud, and government sectors. The data was collected in January and February 2025, with legal professionals making up 41% of respondents.

kp.k: Legal organizational adoption nearly doubled over one year
kp.d: The reported proportion of legal organizations actively using generative AI rose from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025. This measures reported organizational adoption rather than AI's centrality to workflows.
qs: According to the report, 26% of legal organizations are now actively using gen AI, up from 14% in 2024.

kp.k: Workflow centrality is primarily an expectation, not current practice
kp.d: Only 15% of law firm respondents report that generative AI is currently central to their workflow, while 78% expect centrality within five years. Separately, the quoted report refers to 95% of professionals expecting centrality to their organizations' workflows. The headline says over 95% of legal professionals, but the body provides these differently scoped figures; the expectations are not demonstrated future outcomes.
qs: While only 15% of law firm respondents say gen AI is currently central to their workflow, a striking 78% believe it will become central within the next five years.

If 95% of professionals believe GenAI will be central to their organizations’ workflow within the next five years, presumably, new hires today should be present and engaged when GenAI comes to the fore,

kp.k: Other surveys report adoption across different populations and measures
kp.d: Ambrogi places Thomson Reuters' results alongside the ABA's finding that about 21% of law firms used legal-specific generative AI tools; AffiniPay's 31% individual use and 21% organizational adoption at law firms; and Smokeball's reported increase in AI adoption among small and solo firms from 27% in 2023 to 53% in 2024. The article presents these as comparisons, not a single harmonized adoption measure.
qs: The American Bar Association’s Legal Technology Survey Report, which found that about 21% of law firms were using legal-specific gen AI tools.
The 2025 Legal Industry Report published by AffiniPay, which found that individual use of gen AI at law firms was at 31%, though organizational adoption was lower at 21%.
which found that AI adoption among small and solo firms had risen from 27% in 2023 to 53% in 2024.

kp.k: Law firm sentiment shifted toward excitement and hopefulness
kp.d: The survey reports that hesitancy, the predominant law firm reaction in 2024 at 35%, declined to 24% in 2025. Excitement reached 27% and hopefulness 28%, indicating a reported attitudinal shift rather than evidence of improved legal outcomes.
qs: In 2024, hesitancy was the predominant reaction (35%), but in 2025, excitement (27%) and hopefulness (28%) have taken the lead, while hesitancy has dropped to 24%.

kp.k: Document tasks and research lead reported AI uses
kp.d: Document review, legal research and document summarization are the leading reported use cases, at 77%, 74% and 74%, respectively. Nearly 70% of law firm respondents who use generative AI report at least weekly use; this frequency figure concerns users, not all law firm respondents.
qs: Document review (77%), legal research (74%), and document summarization (74%) remain the top use cases for legal professionals. Nearly 70% of law firm respondents who use gen AI report doing so at least weekly.

kp.k: Thomson Reuters frames AI as evolution and expertise augmentation
kp.d: The report characterizes generative AI as evolutionary rather than disruptive to professional work and firm-client interactions. In a separate statement, Thomson Reuters executive Raghu Ramanathan describes legal adoption as enhancing rather than replacing expertise. These are attributed interpretations, not measured findings about employment displacement.
qs: GenAI has not broken the ways professionals work or significantly disrupted the interactions between firms and their clients. Instead, for professional services, it has been more of an evolution.
The legal sector is embracing gen AI not as a threat but as an ally, and this isn’t about replacing legal expertise—it’s about enhancing it.

kp.k: Governance, training, measurement and client awareness lag adoption
kp.d: The report identifies implementation gaps: 41% of law firms have policies governing generative AI, including broader technology policies, and 40% provide staff training. Only 20% of organizations measure tool ROI, while 71% of corporate legal clients do not know whether their outside firms use generative AI.

kp.k: Hiring priorities lag anticipated AI skill needs
kp.d: The report argues that today's new hires should be engaged when generative AI becomes central within five years. It nevertheless observes that a large, unquantified proportion of respondents say their organizations are not targeting applicants with those skills, even after excluding respondents who do not know hiring plans. The quoted observation concerns professionals broadly.

However, even setting aside respondents who don’t know their organization’s hiring plans, a large proportion say their organizations are not targeting applicants with those skills.

kp.k: Report recommends strategic implementation beyond initial adoption
kp.d: As summarized by Ambrogi, the report recommends outcome measurement, governance frameworks and explicit client discussions about when and how generative AI is used as conditions for realizing its potential in legal organizations.
qs: The report concludes that for legal organizations to fully capitalize on gen AI’s potential, they must move beyond initial adoption to strategic implementation, including measuring outcomes, establishing governance frameworks, and having explicit conversations with clients about how and when gen AI is being used.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi reports rising organizational adoption of generative AI and respondents’ expectations that it will become central to legal workflows.
pts.d: Reporting the Thomson Reuters survey, Ambrogi states that active use among legal organizations rose from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025. He distinguishes current centrality to workflow, reported by 15% of law firm respondents, from expected centrality within five years, reported by 78%. These are reported adoption levels and respondent expectations, not measured future outcomes. The headline says 'Over 95%' of legal professionals expect centrality, but the body’s 95% quotation refers to 'professionals' and their organizations, whereas its explicit law-firm-specific figure is 78%; the supplied text does not reconcile these populations or figures.

pts.k: Ambrogi reports increasingly positive sentiment and recurring use concentrated in document review, research, and summarization.
pts.d: The article reports that law firm hesitancy declined from 35% in 2024 to 24% in 2025, while excitement and hopefulness reached 27% and 28%. It identifies document review, legal research, and document summarization as the leading use cases and reports at least weekly use among nearly 70% of law firm respondents who use generative AI. These findings concern attitudes and use patterns, not demonstrated improvements in work quality or productivity.

pts.k: The article presents AI’s effects as evolutionary and augmentative rather than as wholesale disruption or replacement of legal expertise.
pts.d: Ambrogi reproduces the Thomson Reuters report’s characterization of change across professional services as evolutionary, without significant disruption so far to working practices or firm-client interactions. Separately, quoted Thomson Reuters executive Raghu Ramanathan characterizes legal adoption as enhancing rather than replacing expertise and invokes experience with the company’s AI solutions. These are the report’s and Ramanathan’s interpretations relayed by Ambrogi, not independent findings establishing employment effects or the absence of future disruption.

pts.k: Ambrogi reports that adoption is outpacing governance, training, outcome measurement, client communication, and AI-oriented hiring.
pts.d: The article reports implementation gaps: 41% of law firms have policies governing generative AI, 40% provide training, 20% of organizations measure return on investment, and 71% of corporate legal clients do not know whether outside firms use it. It also relays the report’s concern that many organizations are not targeting applicants with AI skills despite expectations of future workflow centrality. Ambrogi reports the conclusion that realizing AI’s potential requires strategic implementation, rather than adoption alone. No quantified causal effect of these measures is supplied.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a cross-sector respondent survey, supplemented by comparisons with other adoption surveys and a vendor executive’s experience-based interpretation.
pts.d: The Thomson Reuters Institute survey covered 1,702 respondents, 41% of whom were legal professionals. Ambrogi also cites ABA findings of about 21% law-firm use of legal-specific generative AI, AffiniPay findings of 31% individual use versus 21% organizational adoption, and Smokeball findings of small and solo firm AI adoption rising from 27% to 53%. These comparisons use different populations and measures, including AI versus generative AI and individual versus organizational use; the article does not establish their direct comparability. The supplied text provides no task-performance benchmarks, measured productivity gains, or detailed legal-subgroup sampling information. Ramanathan’s augmentation claim is supported by his stated experience with Thomson Reuters products, rather than a separately presented replacement study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes early-2025 conditions, changes since 2024, and expected workflow centrality within five years, approximately 2030.
pts.d: Published April 15, 2025, the article draws on January–February 2025 data. Its principal adoption and sentiment comparisons concern 2024–2025; the Smokeball comparison concerns 2023–2024. The five-year claim is a respondent expectation from 2025, not a guaranteed transition. Weekly usage is conditional on already using generative AI. The evolutionary characterization concerns effects observed to date, while the report conditions fuller realization of AI’s potential on governance, outcome measurement, and client communication. It gives no deadline for closing these implementation gaps.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported changes concern legal organizations, practicing professionals, staff and prospective hires, and corporate clients buying outside legal services.
pts.d: Legal professionals are described as incorporating AI into review, research, and summarization. Law firms face policy, training, and implementation needs; staff and new hires are implicated in future AI skills requirements. Corporate legal clients face limited visibility into outside firms’ AI use and are identified as participants in needed disclosure conversations. Small and solo firms appear in a separate adoption-survey comparison, not as a distinct subgroup result from the Thomson Reuters survey. The broader professional-services sample also includes tax, accounting, audit, corporate risk, fraud, and government. The article does not offer concrete claims about access to justice, staffing reductions, billing-model changes, or legal-market redistribution.
